nodes.title: Higher Fitting ideals of a finitely presented module
nodes.statement: Let R be a commutative ring, M a finitely presented R-module and i ≥ 0 an integer. For elements x_1, …, x_n of M with relation module K(x) = {r ∈ R^n : Σ_j r_j·x_j = 0} and for k ≥ 0, let J_k(x) be the ideal of R generated by the minors of size k of all n×k matrices whose columns lie in K(x) (J_0(x) = R); the relation-minors ideal of x in degree i is J_{n−i}(x) for i ≤ n and R for i > n. The i-th Fitting ideal Fitt^i_R(M) is the sum of the relation-minors ideals in degree i of all finite generating families of M. Every generating family gives the whole ideal (API item TauCeti.Module.higherFittingIdeal_eq_relationMinorsIdeal), so that for a finite presentation R^m →A R^n →π M → 0 (π surjective, the columns of the n×m matrix A generating ker π) Fitt^i_R(M) is the ideal generated by the minors of A of size n − i, that is the determinants of the (n − i)×(n − i) submatrices of A, when i < n, and Fitt^i_R(M) = R when i ≥ n. For i = 0 it is the imported initial Fitting ideal Fitt_R(M).
hypotheses: R is an arbitrary commutative ring; no noetherian or finiteness hypothesis is made beyond the stated ones.
M is finitely presented over R, the convention fixed at the start of Appendix B.2 (arXiv v3 PDF p. 93).

Fitt_R(M) = Fitt^0_R(M) is the initial Fitting ideal of a finitely presented R-module M: the ideal generated by the n×n minors of the relation matrix of any finite presentation with n generators, independent of the presentation and compatible with base change. It is the finite-presentation Fitting-ideal carrier imported from the Tau Ceti roadmap StableReduction, Layer 1 (accepted RS-16).

The minor of size 0 is 1, the determinant of the empty matrix, so Fitt^n_R(M) = R is the case of minors of size 0, and Fitt^i_R(M) = R for i > n continues the chain; when n − i exceeds the number m of relations there is no minor and the ideal is 0.

The sum over all generating families is a definition without choices. That one family, or one presentation matrix, already gives the whole ideal is the independence theorem (API items higherFittingIdeal_eq_relationMinorsIdeal and higherFittingIdeal_eq_span_minors); the comparison of Fitt^0 with the imported ideal, base change and localisation follow from it (higherFittingIdeal_zero, higherFittingIdeal_baseChange, higherFittingIdeal_localization). Each is proved in its own node; the proof steps below use none of them.
proofSteps: Matrix form of J_k. If the columns of an n×m matrix A generate K(x), then J_k(x) is the ideal of the k-minors of A: a matrix with columns in K(x) is A·V for some m×k matrix V, and its k-minors are combinations of k-minors of A by the Cauchy–Binet formula for the rectangular matrices A and V (Matrix.compound_mul of PadicMeasuresIwasawaAlgebras:L6/compound-matrix); conversely a k-minor of A is a minor of the matrix formed by k of its columns. For a generating family of a finitely presented module a finite such A exists (Module.FinitePresentation.fg_ker).

J_{k+1}(x) ⊆ J_k(x): by Laplace expansion along a row (Matrix.det_succ_row) a (k + 1)-minor is a combination of k-minors of the matrix obtained by deleting a column, whose columns still lie in K(x). In degrees: the relation-minors ideal in degree i is contained in the one in degree i + 1.

Chain and top degree: summing step 2 over the finite generating families gives Fitt^i_R(M) ⊆ Fitt^{i+1}_R(M). If M has a generating family with n elements and i ≥ n, the term of that family is R, so Fitt^i_R(M) = R.

Monotonicity: for a surjection f : M → M′ of finitely presented modules and a generating family x of M, the family f(x_1), …, f(x_n) generates M′ and K(x) ⊆ K(f(x)), so J_k(x) ⊆ J_k(f(x)) for all k; summing over the families gives Fitt^i_R(M) ⊆ Fitt^i_R(M′). Applied to an isomorphism and its inverse: isomorphic modules have equal Fitting ideals.
acceptance: Fitt^0_R(R/I) = I for a finitely generated ideal I (one generator; the relations are the generators of I): the value of the imported carrier.
Z/2 ⊕ Z/4 over Z: Fitt^0 = (8), Fitt^1 = (2), Fitt^2 = Z; Z ⊕ Z/2: Fitt^0 = 0, Fitt^1 = (2), Fitt^2 = Z.

A module presented by t relations among t + s generators has Fitt^s generated by the t×t minors of its relation matrix: the form used for (171) and for (172), where the source computes all t-column minors of its t×(t + s) matrix for V^θ_p → B^θ_p (arXiv v3 PDF p. 94).

The definition by minors is standard; no further source was read for it. Its independence of the presentation and its base change are not in the source and are separate nodes, with proofs.

nodes.title: A redundant generator shifts the ideals of relation minors
nodes.statement: Let R be a commutative ring, M an R-module, x_1, …, x_n ∈ M and y = Σ_i c_i·x_i with c_i ∈ R; put x′ = (x_1, …, x_n, y). With J_k as in PadicMeasuresIwasawaAlgebras:L6/higher-fitting-ideal (the ideal generated by the k-minors of the matrices with k columns that are relations among the family), J_k(x′) = J_{k−1}(x) for every k ≥ 1. Equivalently x′ and x have the same relation-minors ideal in every degree i ≥ 0: J_{n+1−i}(x′) = J_{n−i}(x) for i ≤ n, and both are R for i > n.
hypotheses: R is an arbitrary commutative ring; no noetherian or finiteness hypothesis is made beyond the stated ones.
M is any R-module and x any finite family, possibly empty; x need not generate M. Only y ∈ Σ_i R·x_i is used.
For k = 0 both J_0(x′) and J_0(x) are R; this is the degree i = n + 1, where the family x has more degree than elements.
proofSteps: Let K ⊆ R^n and K′ ⊆ R^{n+1} be the relation modules of x and x′. The matrix T with T(r, s) = (r + s·c, s) is invertible, with inverse (r, s) ↦ (r − s·c, s), and maps K′ onto K × R, because Σ_i r_i·x_i + s·y = Σ_i (r_i + s·c_i)·x_i.

For an (n + 1)×k matrix B′ with columns in K′, the k-minors of T·B′ are combinations of the k-minors of B′ by the Cauchy–Binet formula (Matrix.compound_mul of PadicMeasuresIwasawaAlgebras:L6/compound-matrix), and conversely with T^{-1}. So J_k(x′) is the ideal generated by the k-minors of the (n + 1)×k matrices with columns in K × R.

A k-minor of such a matrix either avoids the last row, and is a k-minor of an n×k matrix with columns in K, an element of J_k(x); or contains it, and is by expansion along that row (Matrix.det_succ_row) a combination of (k − 1)-minors of matrices with columns in K, an element of J_{k−1}(x). Every generator of J_{k−1}(x) occurs: border an n×(k − 1) matrix with columns in K by the column (0, 1) ∈ K × R and take the minor on the chosen rows and the last row.
J_k(x) ⊆ J_{k−1}(x) (PadicMeasuresIwasawaAlgebras:L6/higher-fitting-ideal, relationMinorsIdeal_le_succ). Hence J_k(x′) = J_{k−1}(x) for k ≥ 1; with k = n + 1 − i this is the degree form for i ≤ n.
acceptance: x empty (n = 0) and y = 0: K′ = R, J_1(x′) = R = J_0(x). This is why the zero module has Fitt^0 = R whether it is generated by no element or by the element 0.

In general, if the columns of A span K, the columns of [[A, −c], [0, 1]] span K′, and the ideal of its k-minors is the ideal of the (k − 1)-minors of A; for A = diag(2, 4) and c = (0, 1) the matrix [[2, 0, 0], [0, 4, −1], [0, 0, 1]] has minors of sizes 3, 2, 1 generating (8), (2), Z.

sources.locator: Appendix B.2, the paragraph before Lemma B.5, arXiv v3 PDF p. 94

This lemma is the step of the standard proof that compares two generating families differing by one redundant generator; it is supplied here and no further source was read for it.

nodes.title: Higher Fitting ideals do not depend on the presentation
nodes.statement: Let R be a commutative ring, M a finitely presented R-module and i ≥ 0. For every finite generating family x_1, …, x_n of M, Fitt^i_R(M) is the relation-minors ideal of x in degree i, that is J_{n−i}(x) for i ≤ n and R for i > n (notation of PadicMeasuresIwasawaAlgebras:L6/higher-fitting-ideal). In matrix form: for every finite presentation R^m →A R^n →π M → 0 (π surjective, the columns of the n×m matrix A generating ker π), Fitt^i_R(M) is the ideal generated by the minors of A of size n − i (R when i ≥ n, 0 when n − i > m). In particular Fitt^0_R(M) is the imported initial Fitting ideal Fitt_R(M).
hypotheses: R is an arbitrary commutative ring; no noetherian or finiteness hypothesis is made beyond the stated ones.
M is finitely presented over R, the convention fixed at the start of Appendix B.2 (arXiv v3 PDF p. 93). The comparison of two generating families uses only that both generate M.

Fitt_R(M) = Fitt^0_R(M) is the initial Fitting ideal of a finitely presented R-module M: the ideal generated by the n×n minors of the relation matrix of any finite presentation with n generators, independent of the presentation and compatible with base change. It is the finite-presentation Fitting-ideal carrier imported from the Tau Ceti roadmap StableReduction, Layer 1 (accepted RS-16).
Fitt^i_R(M) is the higher Fitting ideal of PadicMeasuresIwasawaAlgebras:L6/higher-fitting-ideal: the sum, over all finite generating families of M, of their relation-minors ideals in degree i.
proofSteps: By PadicMeasuresIwasawaAlgebras:L6/relation-minors-add-generator the relation-minors ideal of a family in degree i does not change when an element of the span of the family is appended.

Let x (n elements) and y (p elements) be finite generating families of M. Appending y_1, …, y_p to x one at a time, each a combination of x, and x_1, …, x_n to y, gives the same relation-minors ideals for x and (x, y), and for y and (y, x). The families (x, y) and (y, x) differ by a permutation of coordinates, which permutes the relation modules and changes minors by signs. So x and y have the same relation-minors ideal in every degree.

Fitt^i_R(M) is the sum of these ideals over all finite generating families (PadicMeasuresIwasawaAlgebras:L6/higher-fitting-ideal); they are all equal, and one exists because M is finitely generated. Hence Fitt^i_R(M) is the relation-minors ideal of any one of them.

Matrix form: for x_j = π(e_j) the columns of A generate K(x) = ker π, so J_{n−i}(x) is the ideal of the (n − i)-minors of A (PadicMeasuresIwasawaAlgebras:L6/higher-fitting-ideal, relationMinorsIdeal_eq_span_minors); for n − i > m there is no such minor.
i = 0: J_n(x) is the ideal of the n×n minors of a relation matrix, which is the definition of the imported Fitt_R(M); so Fitt^0_R(M) = Fitt_R(M).

Examples: R^n is presented by n generators and no relation, so its ideal of k-minors is 0 for k ≥ 1 and R for k = 0. R/(a) is presented by the 1×1 matrix (a). R/(a) ⊕ R/(b) is presented by diag(a, b), whose 2-minor is ab and whose 1-minors are a, 0, 0, b.
acceptance: R/(a) presented by one generator with the two relations a, a² (matrix (a, a²)) and by two generators with relation matrix [[a, 0], [0, 1]]: the minors of size 1 of the first and of size 2 of the second both generate (a); the minors of size 0 of the first and of size 1 of the second (a, 0, 0, 1) both generate R.
Z/2 ⊕ Z/4 over Z from diag(2, 4) and from the three-generator presentation [[2, 0, 0], [0, 4, −1], [0, 0, 1]]: both give Fitt^0 = (8), Fitt^1 = (2), Fitt^2 = Z.
The rule matters: with minors of size m − i, m the number of relations, the two presentations of Z/3 by (3, 9) and by [[3, 0], [0, 1]] would give 0, (3), Z and (3), Z, Z.

sources.locator: Appendix B.2, first paragraph, arXiv v3 PDF p. 93
sources.match: The source uses the i-th Fitting ideal of a finitely presented module as a known notion and computes it from one presentation matrix (PDF p. 94). That the ideal of minors does not depend on the presentation is the standard theorem behind this; it is not stated or proved in the source. The proof given here is the standard one, and no further source was read for it.

nodes.title: Higher Fitting ideals commute with base change and localisation
nodes.statement: Let R → R′ be a homomorphism of commutative rings, M a finitely presented R-module and i ≥ 0. Then R′ ⊗_R M is a finitely presented R′-module and Fitt^i_{R′}(R′ ⊗_R M) = Fitt^i_R(M)·R′, the ideal of R′ generated by the image of Fitt^i_R(M). In particular, for a multiplicative subset S of R, Fitt^i_{S^{-1}R}(S^{-1}M) = S^{-1}Fitt^i_R(M).
hypotheses: R is an arbitrary commutative ring; no noetherian or finiteness hypothesis is made beyond the stated ones.
R → R′ is an arbitrary ring homomorphism; no flatness is assumed.
Fitt^i is the higher Fitting ideal of PadicMeasuresIwasawaAlgebras:L6/higher-fitting-ideal; for i = 0 the statement is the base change of the imported carrier.
proofSteps: Choose a finite presentation R^m →A R^n →π M → 0 (Module.FinitePresentation.fg_ker). Applying R′ ⊗_R − gives an exact sequence R′ ⊗_R R^m → R′ ⊗_R R^n → R′ ⊗_R M → 0 whose last map is surjective (lTensor_exact, the right exactness of the tensor product), and under R′ ⊗_R R^k ≅ R′^k its first map is the matrix A′ obtained by applying R → R′ to the entries of A. So R′ ⊗_R M is finitely presented, with n generators and relation matrix A′.

By PadicMeasuresIwasawaAlgebras:L6/higher-fitting-independence, Fitt^i_R(M) is generated by the (n − i)-minors of A and Fitt^i_{R′}(R′ ⊗_R M) by the (n − i)-minors of A′ (both are the unit ideal for i ≥ n). A minor of A′ is the image of the corresponding minor of A (RingHom.map_det). Hence Fitt^i_{R′}(R′ ⊗_R M) = Fitt^i_R(M)·R′.

Localisation is the case R′ = S^{-1}R: S^{-1}M ≅ S^{-1}R ⊗_R M as S^{-1}R-modules (LocalizedModule.equivTensorProduct), and isomorphic modules have the same Fitting ideals (PadicMeasuresIwasawaAlgebras:L6/higher-fitting-ideal, higherFittingIdeal_eq_of_linearEquiv).
acceptance: Z → F_2 and M = Z/2 ⊕ Z/4: F_2 ⊗ M = F_2² is free of rank 2, so its Fitting ideals are 0, 0, F_2; these are the images of (8), (2), Z.
Z → Q and M = Z ⊕ Z/2: Q ⊗ M = Q has Fitting ideals 0, Q; these are the extensions of 0 and (2).
R → R/I and M = R/(a): (R/I) ⊗_R M = (R/I)/(ā) has Fitt^0 = (ā), the image of (a).

sources.locator: Appendix B.2, after (172), arXiv v3 PDF p. 93
sources.match: The source reduces (172), an equality of s-th Fitting ideals over Z[G]^-, to the same equality after tensoring with Z_p[G]^- for every odd prime p, and then computes Fitt^s over Z_p[G]^-. This uses that Fitting ideals commute with base change, which the source does not state. The lemma is standard; its proof is supplied here and no further source was read for it.

nodes.title: Locally quadratic presentations
nodes.statement: A locally quadratic presentation of an R-module M is an exact sequence P_1 →f P_0 →π M → 0 with P_0, P_1 finitely generated projective R-modules of the same constant rank r (rank of (P_i)_𝔭 equal to r at every prime 𝔭). Every quadratic presentation is locally quadratic. Over a ring with finitely many maximal ideals — for instance a local ring, or a finite product of local rings such as Z_p[G], O[G] and the character group rings R_Ψ — a module with a locally quadratic presentation is quadratically presented, because finitely generated projective modules of constant rank over such a ring are free (Dasgupta–Kakde Remark A.7, for Z_p[G]): for r ≥ 1 the presentation becomes R^r → R^r → M → 0 after a choice of bases, and for r = 0 the module M is 0, presented by R →(1) R. An arbitrary Z_p[G]-algebra is not a finite product of local rings (Z_p[G][X] has infinitely many maximal ideals), and over a general ring a locally quadratic presentation need not be quadratic: for a non-principal ideal I of a Dedekind domain R, I ↪ R ↠ R/I is locally quadratic of rank 1, but R/I is not quadratically presented. For the Z_p[G]-algebras R of Remark A.7 the presentation is the base change of the locally quadratic presentation over Z_p[G]; that one is quadratic, and its base change to R is quadratic by QuadraticPresentation.baseChange.
hypotheses: R is an arbitrary commutative ring; no noetherian or finiteness hypothesis is made beyond the stated ones.
Constant rank r means Module.rankAtStalk P 𝔭 = r for every prime 𝔭 of R, the rank of the free R_𝔭-module P_𝔭.
proofSteps: Over a local ring, a finitely generated projective module is flat (Module.Flat.of_projective), hence free (Module.free_of_flat_of_isLocalRing); a free module has rank at every stalk equal to its rank (Module.rankAtStalk_eq_finrank_of_free), so it is free of rank r.

More generally, over a ring R with finitely many maximal ideals a finitely generated projective module of constant rank r is free of rank r (Module.nonempty_basis_of_flat_of_finrank_eq, which asks that (R/𝔪) ⊗_R P have dimension r over R/𝔪 for every maximal ideal 𝔪. Module.rankAtStalk_eq gives the rank at 𝔪 as the dimension of κ(𝔪) ⊗_R P over κ(𝔪), the residue field of the local ring R_𝔪; κ(𝔪) ⊗_R P ≅ κ(𝔪) ⊗_{R/𝔪} ((R/𝔪) ⊗_R P) by TensorProduct.AlgebraTensorModule.cancelBaseChange, and its dimension over κ(𝔪) is the dimension of (R/𝔪) ⊗_R P over the field R/𝔪 by Module.finrank_baseChange). For R = ∏_i A_i with A_i local this is the factorwise statement: P = ∏_i P_i with P_i free over A_i of rank r (step 1 on each factor). Hence P_0 ≅ R^r ≅ P_1, and for r ≥ 1 the presentation becomes R^r → R^r → M → 0.
For r = 0 the module P_0 has rank 0 at every prime, so P_0 = 0 (Module.rankAtStalk_eq_zero_iff_subsingleton) and M = 0, which is quadratically presented by R →(1) R; this needs no hypothesis on R.
A quadratic presentation has P_0 = P_1 = R^m, of constant rank m.

Base change: for a ring map R → R′, tensoring is right exact (lTensor_exact) and preserves finitely generated projective modules and their ranks (Module.rankAtStalk_baseChange), so the base change of a locally quadratic presentation is locally quadratic, and the base change of a quadratic one is quadratic (QuadraticPresentation.baseChange of PadicMeasuresIwasawaAlgebras:L6/quadratic-presentation). This is how Remark A.7 passes from Z_p[G] to a Z_p[G]-algebra.
acceptance: Over Z_p × Z_p the inclusion of Z_p × 0 into R presents 0 × Z_p by projectives of unequal ranks: not locally quadratic.
Over a local ring, locally quadratic of rank r ≥ 1 means quadratic of size r.

uses.how: V^θ → B^θ → ∇ is a locally quadratic presentation of the Ritter–Weiss module
over Z_p[G], a finite product of local rings, the locally quadratic presentation is quadratic (property (P4)); over a Z_p[G]-algebra R the presentation (152) is its base change, hence quadratic
(P4) for ∇ and its base changes to character group rings

tests.statement: R = Z[√−5], I = (2, 1 + √−5): the presentation I ↪ R ↠ R/I is locally quadratic of rank 1 (I is an invertible ideal, hence projective of rank 1), but R/I is not quadratically presented: for a square presentation φ of R/I, comparing the lengths of the cokernel after localising at each prime (where R is a discrete valuation ring) gives (det φ) = I, whereas I is not principal (I has norm 2, and a² + 5b² = 2 has no integer solution). sources.match: Remark A.7; Lemma A.5 (PDF p. 85) uses locally quadratic presentations without separately defining them, and the definition here (finitely generated projective modules of the same constant rank) is read off Lemmas A.4 and A.5. The remark deduces that V^θ_R is free, for a Z_p[G]-algebra R, from the decomposition of Z_p[G] into local factors; R itself need not be one. The statement here reads the remark through base change: V^θ ⊗ Z_p[G] is free, because Z_p[G] satisfies (A2′) for the Σ′ of (59), and V^θ_R is its base change.

nodes.title: Generators and relations of an extension with a quadratically presented quotient
nodes.statement: Let R be a commutative ring and 0 → A → B → C → 0 an exact sequence of R-modules. Let a_1, …, a_n generate A, with relation matrix Ψ of size n×p (its columns generate the module K_A of relations among the a_i), and let C be quadratically presented by (m, φ_C, π_C), with lifts c̃_j ∈ B of the generators π_C(e_j). Let X be an n×m matrix with Σ_j (φ_C)_{jk}·c̃_j = Σ_i X_{ik}·a_i for every k (the k-th lifted relation of C written in the generators of A; such an X exists). Then a_1, …, a_n, c̃_1, …, c̃_m generate B, and the relations among them are generated by the columns of the block upper-triangular matrix [[Ψ, −X], [0, φ_C]] of size (n + m)×(p + m).
hypotheses: R is an arbitrary commutative ring; no noetherian or finiteness hypothesis is made beyond the stated ones.
A is identified with its image in B. Ψ is any matrix whose columns generate the relations among a_1, …, a_n; p need not equal n (p = 0 is allowed), and A need not be quadratically presented.

The proof shows more: without any finite Ψ, the module of relations among (a, c̃) is K_A × 0 plus the span of the m columns (−X_k, (φ_C)_k). So the lemma has a form for a finitely generated A whose relations are not finitely generated.
Exactness is used at A (injectivity of A → B), at B, and at C (surjectivity of B → C, for the lifts c̃_j); of the presentation of C only range φ_C = ker π_C and the surjectivity of π_C are used.
The sign of X comes from moving the lifted relation to the other side; replacing each a_i by −a_i turns −X into X.
proofSteps: Generation: for b ∈ B write the image of b in C as Σ_j y_j·π_C(e_j) (π_C is surjective). Then b − Σ_j y_j·c̃_j maps to 0 in C, so it lies in A (exactness at B) and is a combination of the a_i.

X exists and the columns are relations: for each k, Σ_j (φ_C)_{jk}·c̃_j maps to π_C(φ_C e_k) = 0 in C, hence lies in A and equals Σ_i X_{ik}·a_i for some X_{ik}; so (−X_k, (φ_C)_k) is a relation among (a, c̃), and so is (x, 0) for every x ∈ K_A, in particular for every column of Ψ.

Every relation is a combination of these: if Σ_i x_i·a_i + Σ_j y_j·c̃_j = 0 in B, applying B → C gives Σ_j y_j·π_C(e_j) = 0, so y = φ_C z for some z ∈ R^m (range φ_C = ker π_C). Then Σ_j y_j·c̃_j = Σ_i (Xz)_i·a_i, so Σ_i (x + Xz)_i·a_i = 0 in B, hence in A (A → B is injective), that is x + Xz ∈ K_A. Thus (x, y) = (x + Xz, 0) + (−Xz, φ_C z).
The columns of Ψ generate K_A, so x + Xz = Ψw for some w ∈ R^p and (x, y) = (Ψw, 0) + (−Xz, φ_C z) is a combination of the columns of the block matrix.
acceptance: R = Z, B = Z/9, A = 3Z/9Z with a = 3 and Ψ = (3), C = Z/3 with φ_C = (3) and c̃ = 1: 3·c̃ = 1·a gives X = (1) and the matrix [[3, −1], [0, 3]]. Its columns (3, 0) and (−1, 3) are relations (3·3 = 0 and −3 + 3 = 0 in Z/9), whereas (1, 3) is not (3 + 3 = 6 ≠ 0); the cokernel of the matrix is Z/9.

A non-split extension with A not cyclic and a rectangular Ψ: R = Z, B = Z/2 ⊕ Z/8, a_1 = (1, 0), a_2 = (0, 2), so A ≅ Z/2 ⊕ Z/4, with Ψ = [[2, 0, 2, 0], [0, 4, 4, 8]]; C = B/A ≅ Z/2 with φ_C = (2) and c̃ = (0, 1). Then 2·c̃ = a_2 gives X = (0, 1)ᵀ and the 3×5 matrix [[2, 0, 2, 0, 0], [0, 4, 4, 8, −1], [0, 0, 0, 0, 2]], whose cokernel is Z/2 ⊕ Z/8 (Smith invariants 1, 2, 8), not A ⊕ C.
No relations in A (p = 0): 0 → Z → Z → Z/2 → 0 with first map multiplication by 2, a = 2, c̃ = 1: X = (1) and the 2×1 matrix [[−1], [2]], with cokernel Z.
0 → R/(a) → R/(ab) → R/(b) → 0 for a non-zerodivisor b, the first map being multiplication by b: generators (b, 1) of R/(ab), lifted relation b·1 = 1·b, X = (1), matrix [[a, −1], [0, b]].

sources.locator: Lemma 2.6, arXiv v3 PDF p. 18
sources.match: The source states Lemma 2.6 without argument and cites Northcott, Finite free resolutions, Theorem 22 (not read here). This lemma is the computation of generators and relations on which the direct proofs of both assertions of Lemma 2.6 rest (PadicMeasuresIwasawaAlgebras:L6/quadratic-presentation-extension and PadicMeasuresIwasawaAlgebras:L6/fitting-extension); it is supplied here and is not in the source.

nodes.title: An extension of quadratically presented modules is quadratically presented
nodes.statement: (Dasgupta–Kakde Lemma 2.6, second assertion.) Let R be a commutative ring and 0 → A → B → C → 0 an exact sequence of R-modules with A quadratically presented by (n, ψ_A, π_A) and C quadratically presented by (m, φ_C, π_C). Then B is quadratically presented, of size n + m, by the block upper-triangular matrix [[ψ_A, −X], [0, φ_C]] and the generators a_1, …, a_n, c̃_1, …, c̃_m, where a_i = π_A(e_i), the c̃_j ∈ B are lifts of the π_C(e_j), and X is an n×m matrix with Σ_j (φ_C)_{jk}·c̃_j = Σ_i X_{ik}·a_i for every k. The determinant of this matrix is det ψ_A·det φ_C.
hypotheses: R is an arbitrary commutative ring; no noetherian or finiteness hypothesis is made beyond the stated ones.
A is identified with its image in B. The presentation of B depends on the choice of the lifts c̃_j and of X; its size n + m and its determinant det ψ_A·det φ_C do not.
The sign of X comes from moving the lifted relation to the other side; it does not affect the determinant, and replacing each a_i by −a_i turns −X into X.
proofSteps: By PadicMeasuresIwasawaAlgebras:L6/extension-relation-matrix with Ψ = ψ_A (so p = n), the family a_1, …, a_n, c̃_1, …, c̃_m generates B and its relations are generated by the columns of [[ψ_A, −X], [0, φ_C]].

This matrix is square of size n + m ≥ 1, so together with the surjection R^{n+m} → B it is a quadratic presentation of B (PadicMeasuresIwasawaAlgebras:L6/quadratic-presentation; as data, QuadraticPresentation.ofExact).
Its determinant is det ψ_A·det φ_C (Matrix.det_fromBlocks_zero₂₁).
acceptance: R = Z, B = Z/9, A = 3Z/9Z with a = 3 and ψ_A = (3), C = Z/3 with φ_C = (3) and c̃ = 1: X = (1) and B is presented by [[3, −1], [0, 3]], of size 2 and determinant 9.
0 → R/(a) → R/(ab) → R/(b) → 0 for a non-zerodivisor b, the first map being multiplication by b: R/(ab) is presented by [[a, −1], [0, b]], of determinant ab.

R = Z, B = Z/2 ⊕ Z/8, A = ⟨(1, 0), (0, 2)⟩ ≅ Z/2 ⊕ Z/4 with ψ_A = diag(2, 4), C = B/A ≅ Z/2 with φ_C = (2) and c̃ = (0, 1): X = (0, 1)ᵀ and B is presented by [[2, 0, 0], [0, 4, −1], [0, 0, 2]], of size 3 and determinant 16 = #B.
Split case B = A ⊕ C with c̃_j = (0, c_j): X = 0 and the matrix is block-diagonal (QuadraticPresentation.prod).

sources.locator: Lemma 2.6, arXiv v3 PDF p. 18
sources.match: Lemma 2.6, second assertion. The source gives no argument and cites Northcott, Finite free resolutions, Theorem 22 (not read here). The proof given here applies the block presentation of PadicMeasuresIwasawaAlgebras:L6/extension-relation-matrix to a square relation matrix of A.

nodes.title: Fitting ideals of extensions with a quadratically presented quotient
nodes.statement: (Dasgupta–Kakde Lemma 2.6, first assertion.) Let R be a commutative ring and 0 → A → B → C → 0 an exact sequence of R-modules with C quadratically presented and A finitely presented. Then B is finitely presented and Fitt_R(B) = Fitt_R(A)·Fitt_R(C).
hypotheses: R is an arbitrary commutative ring; no noetherian or finiteness hypothesis is made beyond the stated ones.

Fitt_R(M) = Fitt^0_R(M) is the initial Fitting ideal of a finitely presented R-module M: the ideal generated by the n×n minors of the relation matrix of any finite presentation with n generators, independent of the presentation and compatible with base change. It is the finite-presentation Fitting-ideal carrier imported from the Tau Ceti roadmap StableReduction, Layer 1 (accepted RS-16).

A finitely presented is needed for Fitt_R(A); then B is finitely presented, as an extension of finitely presented modules (Module.finitePresentation_of_ker). The source states the lemma for an arbitrary commutative ring and an arbitrary module A and leaves this implicit (in its applications the modules are finitely generated over noetherian rings) and fixes the convention at the start of Appendix B.2 (arXiv v3 PDF p. 93).
proofSteps: Choose a finite presentation of A, with generators a_1, …, a_n and relation matrix Ψ of size n×p, and a quadratic presentation (m, φ_C, π_C) of C with lifts c̃_j ∈ B of its generators. By PadicMeasuresIwasawaAlgebras:L6/extension-relation-matrix, B is generated by a_1, …, a_n, c̃_1, …, c̃_m with relation matrix the block matrix [[Ψ, −X], [0, φ_C]] of size (n + m)×(p + m). B is finitely presented by Module.finitePresentation_of_ker applied to B → C: C is finitely presented (PadicMeasuresIwasawaAlgebras:L6/quadratic-presentation) and the kernel is isomorphic to A.

Fitt_R(B) is generated by the minors of size n + m of this matrix; such a minor selects all n + m rows and n + m of the columns. If it uses only j < m of the last m columns, the selected square matrix has an m×(n + m − j) block of zeros (the last m rows of the n + m − j columns taken from the first block) with m + (n + m − j) > n + m, so its determinant is 0: in the Leibniz expansion every permutation must send the last m rows into the j remaining columns.

If it uses all of the last m columns and n of the first p, the selected matrix is [[U, −X], [0, φ_C]] with U the n×n matrix formed by n columns of Ψ, and its determinant is det(U)·det(φ_C) by Matrix.det_fromBlocks_zero₂₁. The determinants det(U) generate Fitt_R(A), so Fitt_R(B) = Fitt_R(A)·(det φ_C) = Fitt_R(A)·Fitt_R(C) by PadicMeasuresIwasawaAlgebras:L6/fitting-quadratic.
acceptance: 0 → R/(a) → R/(ab) → R/(b) → 0 for a non-zerodivisor b: (ab) = (a)(b).
Split sequences B = A ⊕ C: Fitt(A ⊕ C) = Fitt(A)Fitt(C) when C is quadratically presented.

The hypothesis on C cannot be dropped: for R = Z[x] and 𝔪 = (2, x), the sequence 0 → 𝔪/𝔪² → R/𝔪² → R/𝔪 → 0 has Fitt_R(B) = 𝔪², Fitt_R(A) = 𝔪² (A ≅ (R/𝔪)²) and Fitt_R(C) = 𝔪, and 𝔪² ≠ 𝔪³ because 4 ∉ 𝔪³; here C = R/𝔪 is not quadratically presented.

sources.locator: Lemma 2.6, arXiv v3 PDF p. 18
sources.match: Lemma 2.6, first assertion, with an explicit finite-presentation hypothesis on A. The source cites Northcott, Finite free resolutions, Theorem 22 (not read here); the proof steps give a direct argument. The second assertion is PadicMeasuresIwasawaAlgebras:L6/quadratic-presentation-extension.

nodes.title: Fitting ideals of two extensions of a common quotient
nodes.statement: (Dasgupta–Kakde Lemma 2.7.) Let B, B′ be quadratically presented R-modules with exact sequences 0 → A → B → C → 0 and 0 → A′ → B′ → C → 0, A and A′ finitely presented. Then Fitt_R(A)·Fitt_R(B′) = Fitt_R(A′)·Fitt_R(B).
hypotheses: R is an arbitrary commutative ring; no noetherian or finiteness hypothesis is made beyond the stated ones.

Fitt_R(M) = Fitt^0_R(M) is the initial Fitting ideal of a finitely presented R-module M: the ideal generated by the n×n minors of the relation matrix of any finite presentation with n generators, independent of the presentation and compatible with base change. It is the finite-presentation Fitting-ideal carrier imported from the Tau Ceti roadmap StableReduction, Layer 1 (accepted RS-16).

A and A′ are finitely presented; then the fibre product B ×_C B′ is finitely presented, as an extension of B by A′. The source leaves this implicit (its modules are finitely generated over noetherian rings, where A and A′ are automatically finitely presented) and fixes the convention in Appendix B.2.
proofSteps: Form M = B ×_C B′, the pairs (b, b′) with the same image in C.

The first projection M → B is surjective because B′ → C is, with kernel {(0, b′) : b′ ↦ 0 in C} ≅ A′; the second projection M → B′ is surjective because B → C is, with kernel ≅ A. So 0 → A′ → M → B → 0 and 0 → A → M → B′ → 0 are exact.

PadicMeasuresIwasawaAlgebras:L6/fitting-extension applied to the first sequence (quotient B quadratically presented, kernel A′ finitely presented) gives Fitt_R(M) = Fitt_R(A′)·Fitt_R(B); applied to the second (quotient B′ quadratically presented, kernel A finitely presented) it gives Fitt_R(M) = Fitt_R(A)·Fitt_R(B′).
acceptance: C = 0: A = B, A′ = B′ and both sides are Fitt(B)Fitt(B′).
B = B′, A = A′: trivial identity.

R = Z, C = Z/2, B = Z/4 and B′ = Z/6 with their reductions to Z/2: A = 2Z/4Z ≅ Z/2, A′ = 2Z/6Z ≅ Z/3, and Fitt(A)·Fitt(B′) = (2)(6) = (12) = (3)(4) = Fitt(A′)·Fitt(B); the fibre product is cyclic of order 12. The other pairing fails: Fitt(A)·Fitt(B) = (8) ≠ (18) = Fitt(A′)·Fitt(B′).

sources.locator: Lemma 2.7 and proof, arXiv v3 PDF p. 18
sources.match: Lemma 2.7 with its fibre-product proof; finite presentation of A and A′ is an explicit hypothesis.

nodes.title: The order of the cokernel of a square matrix over a principal ideal domain
nodes.statement: Let D be a principal ideal domain (possibly a field) and A an m×m matrix over D with det A ≠ 0. Then D^m/AD^m is finite if and only if D/(det A) is finite, and in that case #(D^m/AD^m) = #(D/(det A)).
hypotheses: D is a commutative principal ideal domain; fields, finite or infinite, are allowed. Only det A ≠ 0 is assumed.
With the convention that the cardinality of an infinite quotient is 0 (Nat.card), the statement is the single equality #(D^m/AD^m) = #(D/(det A)).
proofSteps: If D is finite, it is a field (Finite.isField_of_domain) and det A is a unit; then A·adj(A) = det(A)·I (Matrix.mul_adjugate) shows that A is surjective, and both quotients are 0.

Let D be infinite. A is injective on D^m: Av = 0 gives det(A)·v = adj(A)·A·v = 0 (Matrix.adjugate_mul), so v = 0. Hence A is an isomorphism of D^m onto N = AD^m, so N is a submodule of full rank m (finrank N = finrank D^m), and Submodule.quotientEquivPiSpan, applied to N and the standard basis of D^m, gives D^m/AD^m ≅ ∏_{i=1}^m D/(x_i), where x_i is the i-th coefficient Submodule.smithNormalFormCoeffs of N. These coefficients come with a basis b′ of D^m (Submodule.smithNormalFormTopBasis) and a basis of N with the same index set (Submodule.smithNormalFormBotBasis) whose i-th vector is x_i·b′_i (Submodule.smithNormalFormBotBasis_def).

det A is associated to ∏ x_i: the inclusion N ⊆ D^m composed with the isomorphism D^m ≅ N given by A is A, of determinant det A; composed with the isomorphism D^m ≅ N that sends b′_i to the i-th vector x_i·b′_i of the basis of N, it is the endomorphism of D^m that is diagonal with entries x_i in the basis b′, of determinant ∏ x_i. Two composites of the inclusion with isomorphisms D^m ≅ N have associated determinants (LinearMap.associated_det_comp_equiv).

For nonzero a, b in the infinite principal ideal domain D, a Dedekind domain: #(D/(ab)) = #(D/(a))·#(D/(b)), with the value 0 for an infinite quotient (cardQuot_mul). Hence #(D/(det A)) = #(D/(∏ x_i)) = ∏_i #(D/(x_i)) = #(D^m/AD^m), and one side is finite exactly when the other is.
acceptance: D = Z, A = [[2, 1], [0, 3]]: det A = 6 and Z²/AZ² is cyclic of order 6.
D = F_ℓ[t], A = diag(t, t): #(D²/AD²) = ℓ² = #(D/(t²)).
D a field: det A ≠ 0 means that A is invertible, and both quotients are trivial.
m = 1: the statement is the identity #(D/aD) = #(D/(a)).

D = Z: the statement is #(Z^m/AZ^m) = |det A|, which is Mathlib's Submodule.natAbs_det_equiv applied to the isomorphism Z^m ≅ AZ^m given by A; the proof here is the same argument with cardQuot_mul in place of Int.natAbs.

sources.locator: Proof of Lemma 2.4, the case of a PID, arXiv v3 PDF pp. 16–17
sources.match: The first step of the proof of Lemma 2.4, which the source calls well known for PIDs and derives from the Smith normal form. The statement here assumes only det A ≠ 0 and includes fields.

nodes.title: Cokernels of a square matrix over a ring and over a subring of finite index
nodes.statement: Let B be a subring of finite additive index of a commutative ring B′, and let A be an m×m matrix over B whose determinant is a non-zerodivisor of B′. Then (B′)^m/A(B′)^m is finite if and only if B^m/AB^m is finite, and in that case #((B′)^m/A(B′)^m) = #(B^m/AB^m). For m = 1: #(B′/dB′) = #(B/dB) for every d ∈ B that is a non-zerodivisor of B′ (the case of the 1×1 matrix (d), through the isomorphisms B^1/(d)B^1 ≅ B/dB and (B′)^1/(d)(B′)^1 ≅ B′/dB′).
hypotheses: B′ is any commutative ring and B a subring with B′/B finite.

det A is assumed to be a non-zerodivisor of B′, not only of B. The source uses this without stating it, and the conclusion fails without it: for B = {(a, a mod p) : a ∈ Z} ⊂ B′ = Z × F_p and d = (p, 0), a non-zerodivisor of B, #(B′/dB′) = p² and #(B/dB) = p.
proofSteps: Multiplication by A maps (B′)^m onto A(B′)^m and B^m onto AB^m, so it induces a surjection (B′)^m/B^m → A(B′)^m/AB^m. It is injective: if Av = Aw with v ∈ (B′)^m and w ∈ B^m, then det(A)·(v − w) = adj(A)·A·(v − w) = 0 (Matrix.adjugate_mul), so v = w because det A is a non-zerodivisor of B′. Hence [A(B′)^m : AB^m] = [(B′)^m : B^m] = [B′ : B]^m, which is finite and nonzero.

Compare the chains AB^m ⊆ B^m ⊆ (B′)^m and AB^m ⊆ A(B′)^m ⊆ (B′)^m by multiplicativity of the index (the additive form of Subgroup.relIndex_mul_index): [(B′)^m : B^m]·[B^m : AB^m] = [(B′)^m : AB^m] = [(B′)^m : A(B′)^m]·[A(B′)^m : AB^m]. Cancelling the finite nonzero factor of step 1 gives [B^m : AB^m] = [(B′)^m : A(B′)^m], the two indices being finite together.
acceptance: B′ = Z × Z, B = {(a, b) : a ≡ b mod 2}, d = (2, 6): #(B′/dB′) = 12, and #(B/dB) = 12 (B has Z-basis (1, 1), (0, 2) and dB has Z-basis (2, 6), (0, 12)).
B = B′: there is nothing to prove.
B = {(a, a mod p)} ⊂ Z × F_p and d = (p, 0): the hypothesis fails and so does the conclusion (p² ≠ p).

sources.locator: Proof of Lemma 2.4, displays (27) and (28), arXiv v3 PDF p. 17
sources.match: Displays (27) and (28) of the proof of Lemma 2.4, for a subring B of finite index of a ring B′. The hypothesis that det(A) is a non-zerodivisor of B′, which the source uses without stating it, is made explicit (PadicMeasuresIwasawaAlgebras/E18).

nodes.title: The cokernel of a square matrix modulo a finite ideal
nodes.statement: Let B be a commutative ring, K an ideal of B that is finite as a set, and A an m×m matrix over B whose determinant d is a non-zerodivisor of B. Let B̄ = B/K and let Ā be the image of A over B̄. Then (a) the projection B^m → B̄^m induces a bijection B^m/AB^m → B̄^m/ĀB̄^m, so the two quotients are finite together and #(B^m/AB^m) = #(B̄^m/ĀB̄^m); (b) the image d̄ of d is a non-zerodivisor of B̄. For m = 1 and A = (d): #(B/dB) = #(B̄/d̄B̄).
hypotheses: B is any commutative ring and K an ideal with finitely many elements; in the use K = B ∩ ∏(finite factors) for a subring B of a finite product of domains.
Part (a) uses only that multiplication by d is injective on K; part (b) uses that d is a non-zerodivisor of B. Both parts rest on dK = K and are proved together.
The hypothesis on d cannot be dropped: for B = Z × F_p, K = 0 × F_p and A = ((n, 0)) with n ≠ 0, #(B/dB) = p·|n| and #(B̄/d̄B̄) = |n|.
proofSteps: Multiplication by d maps K into K, because K is an ideal, and is injective on K, because d is a non-zerodivisor; an injective self-map of a finite set is bijective, so dK = K.
A maps K^m into K^m. If Av = 0 with v ∈ K^m, then d·v = adj(A)·A·v = 0 (Matrix.adjugate_mul), so v = 0. Hence A is injective, and therefore bijective, on the finite set K^m: AK^m = K^m.
The composite B^m → B̄^m → B̄^m/ĀB̄^m is surjective, and its kernel is K^m + AB^m, which equals AB^m because K^m = AK^m ⊆ AB^m. So it induces a bijection B^m/AB^m → B̄^m/ĀB̄^m. This is (a).
If d·y ∈ K for some y ∈ B, then d·y = d·k for some k ∈ K by the first step, and y = k ∈ K because d is a non-zerodivisor of B (mem_nonZeroDivisors_iff). So d̄·ȳ = 0 implies ȳ = 0 in B̄. This is (b).
acceptance: B = Z × F_p, K = 0 × F_p, A = ((n, 1)) with n ≠ 0: B/dB ≅ Z/n, and B̄ = Z with B̄/nB̄ = Z/n; both have |n| elements.
The hypothesis on d is needed: for B = Z × F_p, K = 0 × F_p and A = ((n, 0)) with n ≠ 0, a zero divisor of B, #(B/dB) = p·|n| while #(B̄/d̄B̄) = |n|.
K = 0: there is nothing to prove.

sources.locator: Proof of Lemma 2.4, arXiv v3 PDF p. 17
sources.match: Not in the source. The source passes from the product B′ to the subring B directly, which can fail when a factor of B′ is a finite field (PadicMeasuresIwasawaAlgebras/E18); this lemma removes the finite factors first, so that the source's passage applies to B/K.

nodes.title: Non-zerodivisors of a finite-index subring of a product of infinite domains
nodes.statement: Let (D_i)_{i∈I} be a family of infinite integral domains, B′ = ∏_{i∈I} D_i, and B a subring of B′ of finite additive index. For x ∈ B the following are equivalent: x is a non-zerodivisor of B; every component x_i ∈ D_i is nonzero; x is a non-zerodivisor of B′.
hypotheses: Each D_i is a commutative domain with infinitely many elements; it need not be a principal ideal domain. The index set is arbitrary; it is finite in the use.
The D_i must be infinite: for B = {(a, a mod p) : a ∈ Z} ⊂ Z × F_p, of index p, the element (p, 0) is a non-zerodivisor of B with a zero component.
proofSteps: Fix i and let δ_i(a) ∈ B′ be the element with component a at i and 0 elsewhere. The map D_i → B′/B, a ↦ δ_i(a) + B, has a finite target and an infinite source, so δ_i(a) − δ_i(b) = δ_i(a − b) ∈ B for some a ≠ b: B contains δ_i(y) with y ≠ 0.
If x is a non-zerodivisor of B, then x·δ_i(y) = δ_i(x_i·y) is nonzero (mem_nonZeroDivisors_iff), so x_i ≠ 0. This holds for every i.
If every x_i is nonzero and x·z = 0 with z ∈ B′, then x_i·z_i = 0 in the domain D_i for every i, so z = 0: x is a non-zerodivisor of B′.
A non-zerodivisor of B′ that lies in B is a non-zerodivisor of the subring B.
acceptance: B = {(a, b) ∈ Z × Z : a ≡ b mod 2}: (2, 0) has a zero component and is a zero divisor of B (it kills (0, 2) ∈ B); (2, 6) is a non-zerodivisor of B and of Z × Z.
B = {(a, a mod p) : a ∈ Z} ⊂ Z × F_p: (p, 0) is a non-zerodivisor of B ≅ Z, has a zero component and is a zero divisor of Z × F_p; the factor F_p is finite, and the equivalence fails.
I empty: B = B′ is the zero ring and all three conditions hold.

sources.locator: Proof of Lemma 2.4, arXiv v3 PDF p. 17
sources.match: Not stated in the source. The source uses det(A), a non-zerodivisor of B, as a non-zerodivisor of the product B′ without proof; this lemma supplies that step when every factor is infinite (PadicMeasuresIwasawaAlgebras/E18).

nodes.title: The order of a quadratically presented module over a finite-index order
nodes.statement: (Dasgupta–Kakde Lemma 2.4.) Let B be a subring of finite index of a finite product B′ = ∏_i D_i of principal ideal domains (fields are allowed; for instance B is a character group ring R_Ψ ⊆ ∏_{ψ∈Ψ} O). Let N be a quadratically presented B-module with Fitt_B(N) = (x) for a non-zerodivisor x of B such that B/(x) is finite. Then N is finite and #N = #(B/(x)).
hypotheses: B ⊆ B′ = ∏_i D_i has finite additive index; each D_i is a principal ideal domain, possibly a field, finite or infinite, of any characteristic. This is the source's generality.

Fitt_R(M) = Fitt^0_R(M) is the initial Fitting ideal of a finitely presented R-module M: the ideal generated by the n×n minors of the relation matrix of any finite presentation with n generators, independent of the presentation and compatible with base change. It is the finite-presentation Fitting-ideal carrier imported from the Tau Ceti roadmap StableReduction, Layer 1 (accepted RS-16).
When every D_i is infinite, in particular in characteristic zero, which covers every use (R_Ψ ⊆ ∏ O), the ideal K of the proof is 0 and x is already a non-zerodivisor of B′.
proofSteps: Let A be the m×m relation matrix, so N ≅ B^m/AB^m and (det A) = (x) by PadicMeasuresIwasawaAlgebras:L6/fitting-quadratic. As x is a non-zerodivisor, d = det A is a unit multiple of x; so d is a non-zerodivisor of B, B/dB = B/(x) is finite, and it suffices to show that B^m/AB^m is finite with #(B^m/AB^m) = #(B/dB).

Reduction to infinite factors. Write B′ = D × F, with D the product of the infinite D_i and F the product of the finite ones, and let K = B ∩ (0 × F), the kernel of the projection B → D: a finite ideal of B. By PadicMeasuresIwasawaAlgebras:L6/cokernel-modulo-finite-ideal, applied to A and to the 1×1 matrix (d): #(B^m/AB^m) = #((B/K)^m/A(B/K)^m) and #(B/dB) = #((B/K)/d(B/K)), each pair being finite together, and the image of d in B/K is a non-zerodivisor.

B/K is the image of B in D, a subring of finite index of D (the quotient of D by it is a quotient of B′/B), and the determinant of the image of A is the image of d. So it suffices to treat the case in which every D_i is infinite, where K = 0.
Assume every D_i infinite. By PadicMeasuresIwasawaAlgebras:L6/finite-index-subring-nonzerodivisor, every component d_i of d is nonzero and d is a non-zerodivisor of B′.

By PadicMeasuresIwasawaAlgebras:L6/finite-index-cokernel-descent, applied to A and to the 1×1 matrix (d): #(B^m/AB^m) = #((B′)^m/A(B′)^m) and #(B/dB) = #(B′/dB′), each pair being finite together. In particular B′/dB′ = ∏_i D_i/(d_i) is finite.

By PadicMeasuresIwasawaAlgebras:L6/pid-cokernel-cardinality on each factor (the i-th component A_i of A has det A_i = d_i ≠ 0 and D_i/(d_i) is finite): #(D_i^m/A_iD_i^m) = #(D_i/(d_i)). Taking the product over i gives #((B′)^m/A(B′)^m) = #(B′/dB′). Hence #N = #(B^m/AB^m) = #(B′/dB′) = #(B/dB) = #(B/(x)).
acceptance: B a discrete valuation ring with finite residue field, a ≠ 0, N = B/(a): #N = #(B/(a)) (the 1×1 presentation (a)).
N = 0 with presentation (1): #N = 1 = #(B/B).

B = Z[C_2] = Z[h]/(h² − 1) ≅ {(a, b) ∈ Z × Z : a ≡ b mod 2} and A = [[1 + h, 1 − h], [1 − h, 1 + h]]: det A = 4h, so Fitt_B(N) = (4) for N = B²/AB². As a group N ≅ Z/2 ⊕ Z/2 ⊕ Z/4, of order 16 = #(B/4B), although N is not isomorphic to B/4B ≅ (Z/4)².

A finite-field factor with K = 0: B = {(a, a mod 2) : a ∈ Z} ⊂ Z × F_2 and A = [[(2, 0), (1, 1)], [(0, 0), (1, 1)]]. Then det A = x = (2, 0) is a non-zerodivisor of B and a zero divisor of Z × F_2, and #N = 2 = #(B/(x)), whereas over B′ = Z × F_2 both counts are 4: #((B′)²/A(B′)²) = 4 = #(B′/xB′). The order is computed over B, not over the product.
A finite-field factor with K ≠ 0: B = B′ = Z × F_2 and A = [[(2, 1), (1, 0)], [(0, 1), (3, 1)]]: det A = (6, 1), K = 0 × F_2, B/K = Z and #N = 6 = #(B/(x)).

m = 1 with a finite-field factor: for B = {(a, a mod p) : a ∈ Z} ⊂ Z × F_p and x = (p, 0), or B = Z × F_p and x = (n, 1) with n ≠ 0, the module N = B/(x) has order p, respectively |n|; here the statement is the definition of N, and the examples only show K = 0, respectively K = 0 × F_p.

sources.locator: Lemma 2.4, arXiv v3 PDF p. 16–17
sources.match: Lemma 2.4 in the source's generality. The source's proof applies displays (27)–(28) with det(A) known to be a non-zerodivisor of B only; that step can fail when a factor is a finite field (PadicMeasuresIwasawaAlgebras/E18). The proof here first divides by the finite ideal K = B ∩ ∏(finite factors) and then follows the source.

nodes.title: Compound matrices
nodes.statement: For a commutative ring R, finite linearly ordered index types and an ι×κ matrix A over R, the r-th compound matrix C_r(A) is the matrix indexed by r-subsets S ⊆ ι and T ⊆ κ whose (S, T) entry is the minor det A[S, T] (rows S and columns T in increasing order). It is the matrix of ⋀^r A : ⋀^r R^κ → ⋀^r R^ι in the bases e_T = e_{t_1} ∧ … ∧ e_{t_r} (t_1 < … < t_r) of Mathlib's exterior-power bases.
hypotheses: R is an arbitrary commutative ring; no noetherian or finiteness hypothesis is made beyond the stated ones.
Index types are finite and linearly ordered; r-subsets are Set.powersetCard, enumerated increasingly by the inverse of Set.powersetCard.ofFinEmbEquiv.
proofSteps: Define the entry as the determinant of A.submatrix along the increasing enumerations of S and T (the inverse of Set.powersetCard.ofFinEmbEquiv). For r = 1 the bijection of an index type with its 1-subsets is Set.powersetCard.ofSingleton, and C_1(A)_{{i},{k}} = A_{ik}.

The basis vector e_T of Module.Basis.exteriorPower is the wedge of e_{t_1}, …, e_{t_r}, so ⋀^r A(e_T) is the wedge of A e_{t_1}, …, A e_{t_r} (exteriorPower.map_apply_ιMulti). Its e_S-coordinate is the value of the functional exteriorPower.ιMultiDual at S (exteriorPower.basis_repr_apply), which exteriorPower.ιMultiDual_apply_ιMulti computes as the determinant of the matrix (i, j) ↦ (A e_{t_i})_{s_j} = A_{s_j, t_i}; this is the transpose of A[S, T], and Matrix.det_transpose gives det A[S, T]. This is compound_eq_toMatrix (LinearMap.toMatrix of ⋀^r of Matrix.toLin' A in the two exterior-power bases).

Cauchy–Binet: toLin'(AB) = toLin'(A) ∘ toLin'(B) (Matrix.toLin'_mul), functoriality of exterior powers (exteriorPower.map_comp) and LinearMap.toMatrix_comp give C_r(AB) = C_r(A)C_r(B). C_r(1) = 1 because det 1[S, T] is 1 for S = T and has a zero row otherwise.

Column restriction: for an order embedding e : J → κ write A·e for the ι×J matrix with entries (A·e)_{i,j} = A_{i,e(j)} (A.submatrix id e). For an r-subset T of J the increasing enumeration of e(T) is e composed with that of T, so C_r(A·e)_{S,T} and C_r(A)_{S,e(T)} are the determinant of the same submatrix. For an injection e that is not monotone the two differ by the sign of the permutation that sorts e on the enumeration of T.

Transpose and special cases: C_r(Aᵀ) = C_r(A)ᵀ by Matrix.det_transpose. For r = 2 the entries are the pinned 2×2 minors Matrix.pairMinor and Cauchy–Binet is Matrix.pairMinor_mul; for square A of size m, C_m(A) = (det A) is the matrix form of the pinned exteriorPower.map_top_eq_det_smul.
acceptance: C_1(A) = A under the bijections of ι and of κ with their 1-subsets.
For square A of size m, C_m(A) = (det A).

nodes.title: The sign of the shuffle of a subset with its complement
nodes.statement: Let 0 ≤ r ≤ m and let T be an r-subset of Fin m with elements t_0 < … < t_{r−1} and complement Tᶜ = {u_0 < … < u_{m−r−1}}. The permutation Set.powersetCard.permOfDisjoint of Fin (r + (m − r)) attached to the disjoint pair (T, Tᶜ), which sends position k < r to the rank of t_k and position r + l to the rank of u_l in T ∪ Tᶜ = Fin m, has sign (−1)^{ΣT − r(r−1)/2}, where ΣT = t_0 + … + t_{r−1} is the sum of the elements of T as natural numbers, so that ΣT ≥ r(r − 1)/2. Consequently, for every family (v_i)_{i ∈ Fin m} of elements of a module, v_T ∧ v_{Tᶜ} = (−1)^{ΣT − r(r−1)/2}·v_0 ∧ … ∧ v_{m−1} in the exterior algebra, where v_U is the wedge of the v_i, i ∈ U, in increasing order.
hypotheses: m and r are natural numbers with r ≤ m, so that the complement is an (m − r)-subset (Set.powersetCard.compl); the sign statement involves no ring.
The elements of Fin m are summed as the natural numbers 0, …, m − 1. With labels 1, …, m the sum grows by r and the exponent is ΣT − r(r + 1)/2.
proofSteps: Write σ for the permutation. Because T ∪ Tᶜ is all of Fin m, the rank of an element in the sorted union is the element itself; so, unfolding Set.powersetCard.permOfDisjoint, σ(k) = t_k for k < r and σ(r + l) = u_l for l < m − r.

Inversions of σ, that is pairs of positions i < j with σ(j) < σ(i): there is none inside the first block and none inside the second, because both enumerations are increasing. A pair (k, r + l) is an inversion iff u_l < t_k. For fixed k the number of such l is the number of elements of Tᶜ below t_k, which is t_k − k: of the t_k elements of Fin m below t_k exactly k, namely t_0, …, t_{k−1}, lie in T.
So σ has Σ_{k<r} (t_k − k) = ΣT − r(r − 1)/2 inversions, and its sign is (−1) to that number (TauCeti.sign_eq_neg_one_pow_card_inversion).
The consequence is ExteriorAlgebra.ιMulti_family_mul_of_disjoint for the pair (T, Tᶜ), whose union is Fin m.
acceptance: m = 3, T = {1}: the list 1, 0, 2 has one inversion, ΣT − 0 = 1, and e_1 ∧ (e_0 ∧ e_2) = −e_0 ∧ e_1 ∧ e_2.
m = 4, T = {1, 3}: the list 1, 3, 0, 2 has three inversions and ΣT − 1 = 3; the sign is −1.
T = {0, …, r − 1}: ΣT = r(r − 1)/2 and the permutation is the identity; so are the cases r = 0 and r = m.
For two r-subsets S, T the product of the two signs is (−1)^{ΣS+ΣT}, because r(r − 1) is even.

sources.locator: Proof of Lemma 3.9, arXiv v3 PDF p. 26
sources.match: Not in the source, which uses the higher adjugate without defining it; this sign is what the entry rule of adj_r and the generalised Laplace expansion need.

nodes.title: Generalised Laplace expansion along a set of rows
nodes.statement: Let A be an m×m matrix over a commutative ring R, 0 ≤ r ≤ m, and S, S′ two r-subsets of Fin m. Then Σ_T (−1)^{ΣS′+ΣT}·det A[S, T]·det A[S′ᶜ, Tᶜ] is det A if S′ = S and 0 if S′ ≠ S. The sum is over the r-subsets T of Fin m, ΣT is the sum of the elements of T, and A[U, V] is the submatrix on the rows U and the columns V in increasing order. For S′ = S this is the Laplace expansion of det A along the rows S; for S′ ≠ S it is the expansion of a determinant with a repeated row.
hypotheses: R is an arbitrary commutative ring; no noetherian or finiteness hypothesis is made beyond the stated ones.
Indices are Fin m and r ≤ m, so that complements are (m − r)-subsets (Set.powersetCard.compl); with 0-based or 1-based element sums the sign (−1)^{ΣS′+ΣT} is the same, since both change by 2r.
proofSteps: Let ρ_i ∈ R^m be the i-th row of A and, for a subset U of Fin m, ρ_U the wedge of the ρ_i, i ∈ U, in increasing order. Since ρ_i = Aᵀe_i, ρ_U is the image of e_U under ⋀ of Aᵀ (exteriorPower.map_apply_ιMulti), and by compound-matrix for the transpose of A (compound_eq_toMatrix, compound_transpose), ρ_U = Σ_V det A[U, V] e_V, the sum over the subsets V with as many elements as U.

Expand ρ_S ∧ ρ_{S′ᶜ} = Σ_{T,V} det A[S, T] det A[S′ᶜ, V] e_T ∧ e_V, T running over the r-subsets and V over the (m − r)-subsets. The terms with V ≠ Tᶜ vanish (ExteriorAlgebra.ιMulti_family_mul_of_not_disjoint), and e_T ∧ e_{Tᶜ} = ε(T) e_0 ∧ … ∧ e_{m−1} with ε(T) = (−1)^{ΣT − r(r−1)/2} (PadicMeasuresIwasawaAlgebras:L6/complement-shuffle-sign). So ρ_S ∧ ρ_{S′ᶜ} = (Σ_T ε(T) det A[S, T] det A[S′ᶜ, Tᶜ])·e_0 ∧ … ∧ e_{m−1}.

If S′ = S, the same sign lemma for the family ρ gives ρ_S ∧ ρ_{Sᶜ} = ε(S) ρ_0 ∧ … ∧ ρ_{m−1} = ε(S) det(A) e_0 ∧ … ∧ e_{m−1}: by exteriorPower.ιMulti_eq_basis_det_smul the top wedge of the family ρ is its determinant against the standard basis, det Aᵀ = det A (Matrix.det_transpose), times the top wedge of the basis. If S′ ≠ S, some i lies in S and in S′ᶜ, because both have r elements, and ρ_S ∧ ρ_{S′ᶜ} = 0 (ExteriorAlgebra.ιMulti_family_mul_of_not_disjoint).
Compare the coefficients of the basis vector e_0 ∧ … ∧ e_{m−1} of ⋀^m R^m (Module.Basis.exteriorPower) and multiply by ε(S′): ε(S′)ε(T) = (−1)^{ΣS′+ΣT} and ε(S′)² = 1.
acceptance: r = 1, S = S′ = {i}: det A = Σ_j (−1)^{i+j} A_{ij}·det A[{i}ᶜ, {j}ᶜ], the expansion along the row i.
r = m: the only T is Fin m and the formula reads det A = det A; r = 0: the only T is empty and it reads det A = det A[Fin m, Fin m].
m = 4, r = 2, S = S′ = {0, 1}: det A = Σ_T (−1)^{1+ΣT} det A[{0,1}, T]·det A[{2,3}, Tᶜ], the sum over the six 2-subsets T of the columns.

nodes.title: Higher adjugates
nodes.statement: For a square m×m matrix A over a commutative ring and 0 ≤ r ≤ m, the r-th higher adjugate adj_r(A) is the matrix indexed by r-subsets with entry adj_r(A)_{T,S} = (−1)^{ΣS+ΣT} det A[Sᶜ, Tᶜ] (complementary minor; ΣS the sum of the elements of S). It satisfies C_r(A)·adj_r(A) = det(A)·I and adj_r(A)·C_r(A) = det(A)·I (generalized Laplace expansion); adj_1 is the adjugate and adj_m = (1).
hypotheses: R is an arbitrary commutative ring; no noetherian or finiteness hypothesis is made beyond the stated ones.
Indices are Fin m; with 0-based or 1-based element sums the sign is the same, since both change by 2r.
proofSteps: Define the entry from the complements S ↦ Sᶜ (Set.powersetCard.compl, which needs (m − r) + r = m, that is r ≤ m) and the increasing enumerations.

(C_r(A)adj_r(A))_{S,S′} = Σ_T (−1)^{ΣS′+ΣT} det A[S, T] det A[S′ᶜ, Tᶜ], which is det A for S′ = S and 0 for S′ ≠ S by the generalised Laplace expansion (PadicMeasuresIwasawaAlgebras:L6/generalised-laplace-expansion); so C_r(A)·adj_r(A) = det(A)·I.
adj_r(Aᵀ) = adj_r(A)ᵀ (Matrix.det_transpose) and C_r(Aᵀ) = C_r(A)ᵀ (compound-matrix, compound_transpose), so the transpose of the identity for Aᵀ is adj_r(A)·C_r(A) = det(A)·I.

For r = 1 the increasing enumeration of {i}ᶜ is Fin.succAbove i (Finset.orderEmbOfFin_compl_singleton_eq_succAboveOrderEmb), and Matrix.adjugate_fin_succ_eq_det_submatrix (adjugate A j i = (−1)^{i+j} det A with row i and column j deleted) gives adj_1(A)_{{j},{i}} = adjugate(A)_{j,i}; the two identities are then Matrix.mul_adjugate and Matrix.adjugate_mul.
For r = m the complements are empty and adj_m(A) = (1); for r = 0, S = T = ∅ and adj_0(A) = (det A).
acceptance: r = m: the complementary minor is empty and adj_m(A) = (1).

uses.how: det(A′)x = C_r(A′)·adj_r(A′)·x puts det(A′)x in the image of C_r(A) (the identity with adj_r on the right)
its first step is the identity C_r(A_J)·adj_r(A_J) = det(A_J)·I (Matrix.compound_mul_higherAdjugate)

nodes.title: A maximal minor times a vector lies in the image of the compound matrix
nodes.statement: Let R be a commutative ring, A an m×n matrix over R, e : Fin m → Fin n an order embedding, A_J = A·e the m×m submatrix of A on the columns J = e(Fin m), and r ≤ m. For every vector x indexed by the r-subsets of Fin m, the vector det(A_J)·x lies in the image of C_r(A) : R^{(n choose r)} → R^{(m choose r)}; explicitly det(A_J)·x = C_r(A)(ι_J(adj_r(A_J)x)), where ι_J extends a vector indexed by the r-subsets of Fin m by zero along T ↦ e(T).
hypotheses: R is an arbitrary commutative ring; no noetherian or finiteness hypothesis is made beyond the stated ones.

Rows and columns are indexed by Fin m and Fin n, and J is given by an order embedding, so that the increasing enumeration of e(T) is e composed with that of T. The existence of e forces m ≤ n; r = 0 is allowed.
proofSteps: C_r(A_J)·adj_r(A_J) = det(A_J)·I (higher-adjugate, the identity with adj_r on the right, compound_mul_higherAdjugate), so det(A_J)·x = C_r(A_J)(adj_r(A_J)x).
C_r(A_J)_{S,T} = C_r(A)_{S,e(T)} (compound-matrix, compound_submatrix_col) and T ↦ e(T) is injective, so C_r(A_J)·y = C_r(A)·ι_J(y) for every y; take y = adj_r(A_J)x.
acceptance: r = 1: det(A_J)·x = A·ι_J(adj(A_J)x), Cramer's rule on the columns J.
r = m: adj_m(A_J) = (1), C_m(A) is the row of the maximal minors of A, and the identity reads det(A_J)·x = det(A_J)·x.
r = 0: C_0(A) = (1) and adj_0(A_J) = (det A_J).

sources.locator: Proof of Lemma 3.9, last step, arXiv v3 PDF p. 26
sources.match: The last step of the source's proof, for free modules. The source's display applies adj_r(A′) to C_r(A)x̃, an element of the image; the step here uses the identity with adj_r on the right and the vector adj_r(A′)x extended by zero (PadicMeasuresIwasawaAlgebras/E17).

nodes.title: Fitting ideals annihilate exterior-power cokernels
nodes.statement: (Dasgupta–Kakde Lemma 3.9.) Let R be a commutative ring and N ⊆ M R-modules with N finitely generated and M finitely presented. For every r ≥ 1, Fitt_R(M/N) annihilates the cokernel of ⋀^r_R N → ⋀^r_R M.
hypotheses: R is an arbitrary commutative ring; no noetherian or finiteness hypothesis is made beyond the stated ones.

Fitt_R(M) = Fitt^0_R(M) is the initial Fitting ideal of a finitely presented R-module M: the ideal generated by the n×n minors of the relation matrix of any finite presentation with n generators, independent of the presentation and compatible with base change. It is the finite-presentation Fitting-ideal carrier imported from the Tau Ceti roadmap StableReduction, Layer 1 (accepted RS-16).
M/N is finitely presented, because M is finitely presented and N is finitely generated; so Fitt_R(M/N) is defined.
proofSteps: M/N is finitely presented (Module.finitePresentation_of_surjective: M is finitely presented and the kernel N of M ↠ M/N is finitely generated). Choose p : R^m ↠ M. The kernel of R^m ↠ M ↠ M/N is finitely generated (Module.FinitePresentation.fg_ker), so it is the image of some A : R^n → R^m. The composite R^n → R^m → M → M/N is zero, so p∘A takes values in N.

By exteriorPower.map_comp the image of ⋀^r R^n → ⋀^r R^m → ⋀^r M lies in the image of ⋀^r N → ⋀^r M, and ⋀^r R^m → ⋀^r M is surjective (exteriorPower.map_surjective). So the cokernel C_2 of ⋀^r A maps onto the cokernel C_1 of ⋀^r N → ⋀^r M, and it suffices that Fitt(M/N) kills C_2.

R^n → R^m → M/N → 0 is a finite presentation with m generators, so Fitt(M/N) is generated by the m×m minors det(A_J) of the m×n matrix A, J running over the m-subsets of the n columns. If n < m there is no such minor, Fitt(M/N) = 0 and nothing is to prove.

If r > m, then ⋀^r R^m = 0, because its basis Module.Basis.exteriorPower is indexed by the r-subsets of Fin m and there is none; so C_2 = 0. If r ≤ m: in the exterior-power bases ⋀^r A is the compound matrix C_r(A) (compound-matrix, compound_eq_toMatrix), and for every x ∈ ⋀^r R^m and every m-subset J of the n columns, given by its increasing enumeration e : Fin m → Fin n, the element det(A_J)x lies in the image of C_r(A) (PadicMeasuresIwasawaAlgebras:L6/compound-image-determinant, which assumes r ≤ m). So every generator of Fitt(M/N) kills C_2.
acceptance: r = 1: Fitt(M/N)·M ⊆ N, i.e. Fitt ⊆ Ann(M/N).
N = M: the cokernel is 0 and Fitt(0) = R.
r = 0: both exterior powers are R and the cokernel is 0, so the statement holds trivially.

R = Z, M = Z², N = 2Z ⊕ 4Z: Fitt(M/N) = (8). For r = 2 the image of ⋀²N → ⋀²M = Z is generated by 2e_1 ∧ 4e_2, the cokernel is Z/8 and its annihilator is exactly (8); for r = 1 the cokernel Z/2 ⊕ Z/4 has annihilator (4) ⊋ (8).

sources.locator: Lemma 3.9, arXiv v3 PDF p. 25–26
sources.match: Statement of Lemma 3.9. The reduction to free modules follows the source; the last step of the source's proof is PadicMeasuresIwasawaAlgebras:L6/compound-image-determinant, where its display is corrected (PadicMeasuresIwasawaAlgebras/E17).

nodes.title: The transpose of a finite projective presentation
nodes.statement: For a commutative ring R, a ring isomorphism σ : S → R, and a presentation P_1 →f P_0 → M → 0 by finitely generated projective R-modules, the transpose attached to it is M^tr = coker(f^* : P_0^* → P_1^*), an S-module through the contragredient structure (for R = R_Ψ, S = R^# and σ = #). Its carrier is the pinned Tau Ceti cokernel TauCeti.AuslanderReitenTranspose f (any ring, any presentation map), with scalars restricted along σ. The transpose depends on the presentation, not on M alone: for a square presentation with matrix (a_ij) it is quadratically presented over S by (σ^{-1}(a_ji)). Dasgupta–Kakde write the presentation as P_0 → P_1 → M with the indices swapped.
hypotheses: R is an arbitrary commutative ring; no noetherian or finiteness hypothesis is made beyond the stated ones.

Minimal presentations, the stable category and the translate D Tr (Tau Ceti QuiverRepresentations Layer 6) are not used or rebuilt here. The pinned uniqueness theorem (TauCeti.IsMinimalProjectivePresentation.nonempty_linearEquiv_auslanderReitenTranspose) compares two minimal projective presentations, over any ring; the presentations of Dasgupta–Kakde are not assumed minimal, and over Z[G] minimal presentations need not exist (Z/2 has no projective cover over Z).
proofSteps: Reuse TauCeti.AuslanderReitenTranspose f, the cokernel of f.lcomp : Module.Dual R P_0 → Module.Dual R P_1 (LinearMap.lcomp), an R^op-module. The pinned file does not expose this definition, so every construction on it goes through its API: the quotient map mk with mk_eq_zero_iff, mk_surjective and induction_on, the universal property lift with lift_mk and hom_ext, and linearEquiv with linearEquiv_mk. For commutative R the pinned module structure over a commutative base ring k of the coefficient ring, taken with k = R, is its R-module structure; it is the R^op-structure read through r ↦ op r (TauCeti.AuslanderReitenTranspose.op_algebraMap_smul with k = R). An element s ∈ S acts as σ(s) (Module.compHom along σ).
Isomorphic presentations give isomorphic transposes by TauCeti.AuslanderReitenTranspose.linearEquiv; on classes it is φ ↦ φ ∘ e_1^{-1} (linearEquiv_mk), which commutes with the action of S.

Adding an identity summand Q → Q leaves the transpose unchanged; adding a relation summand Q → 0 adds Q^*: (P ⊕ Q)^* = P^* ⊕ Q^* (Module.dualProdDualEquivDual), the maps in both directions are defined by lift and compared on classes by lift_mk and induction_on.
For R^m →φ R^m, given by Matrix.toLin' of the relation matrix, f^* in the dual bases is the transpose matrix (LinearMap.toMatrix_transpose); transporting along σ^{-1} gives (σ^{-1}(a_ji)).

Base change: for P finitely generated projective, R′ ⊗_R P^* ≅ (R′ ⊗_R P)^* (TauCeti.Module.Dual.baseChangeEvaluationEquiv), and these isomorphisms for P_0 and P_1 carry R′ ⊗ f^* to the dual of f ⊗ R′ = LinearMap.baseChange R′ f (naturality of the evaluation, Module.Dual.baseChangeEvaluation_one_tmul_baseChange). Base change is right exact (lTensor_exact), so R′ ⊗_R coker(f^*) is the cokernel of R′ ⊗ f^*, hence of (f ⊗ R′)^*. For an R-module X regarded as an S-module through σ, S′ ⊗_S X ≅ R′ ⊗_R X by s′ ⊗ x ↦ σ′(s′) ⊗ x, because σ and σ′ are isomorphisms compatible with S → S′ and R → R′; it carries the S′-structure of the left side to the structure through σ′ of the right side.
acceptance: The presentation R →(1) R of 0 has transpose 0; the presentation R² → R, (a, b) ↦ a, of 0 has transpose ≅ S.
R →(a) R presents R/(a), with transpose S/(σ^{-1}(a)).

nodes.title: Transposes are unique up to projective summands
nodes.statement: If P_1 →f P_0 →π M → 0 and Q_1 →g Q_0 →ρ M → 0 are presentations by finitely generated projective R-modules, then tr(f) ⊕ (Q_1 ⊕ P_0)^* ≅ tr(g) ⊕ (P_1 ⊕ Q_0)^* as S-modules; in particular the two transposes M′ = tr(f) and M″ = tr(g) of M satisfy M′ ⊕ P ≅ M″ ⊕ Q with P = (Q_1 ⊕ P_0)^* and Q = (P_1 ⊕ Q_0)^* finitely generated projective S-modules.
hypotheses: R is an arbitrary commutative ring; no noetherian or finiteness hypothesis is made beyond the stated ones.

The stable module category and the duality Tr of Tau Ceti QuiverRepresentations Layer 6 (sublayer 6C: finite-dimensional algebras, minimal projective presentations) are not rebuilt. This node compares two arbitrary finite projective presentations over a commutative ring, which the pinned uniqueness theorem for minimal presentations (TauCeti.IsMinimalProjectivePresentation.nonempty_linearEquiv_auslanderReitenTranspose) does not give. The argument of the proof steps uses commutativity only for S-linearity and through the Mathlib lemmas on duals of products and of finitely generated projective modules (Module.dualProdDualEquivDual, Module.dual_projective, Module.dual_finite), which are stated over commutative rings; a noncommutative version is not planned here.
proofSteps: Put E = P_0 ⊕ Q_0 and K = ker((π, ρ) : E → M). Choose β : Q_0 → P_0 with πβ = ρ (Module.projective_lifting_property). Then u : P_1 ⊕ Q_0 → E, (x, y) ↦ (f x − β y, y), has image K: it lands in K because π(f x − β y) + ρ y = 0, and for (p, q) ∈ K one has π(p + β q) = 0, so p + β q = f x and u(x, q) = (p, q). It is f ⊕ id_{Q_0} followed by the automorphism (p, q) ↦ (p − β q, q) of E, so tr(u) ≅ tr(f ⊕ id_{Q_0}) ≅ tr(f) (presentation-transpose: equivOfIso, equivAddId). In the same way, with β′ : P_0 → Q_0, ρβ′ = π, the map v : Q_1 ⊕ P_0 → E, (x′, y′) ↦ (y′, g x′ − β′ y′), has image K and tr(v) ≅ tr(g).

Let u : F_1 → E and v : F_2 → E be maps from projective modules with the same image K; transposes are taken of these maps into E. Choose s : F_2 → F_1 with u s = v (Module.projective_lifting_property for F_1 ↠ K). Then (u, v) : F_1 ⊕ F_2 → E is (u, 0) composed with the automorphism (x, y) ↦ (x + s y, y), so tr(u, v) ≅ tr(u, 0) ≅ tr(u) ⊕ F_2^* (equivOfIso, equivAddZero). Exchanging the roles of u and v, and the two summands of F_1 ⊕ F_2, tr(u, v) ≅ tr(v) ⊕ F_1^*.

With F_1 = P_1 ⊕ Q_0 and F_2 = Q_1 ⊕ P_0: tr(f) ⊕ (Q_1 ⊕ P_0)^* ≅ tr(u) ⊕ F_2^* ≅ tr(u, v) ≅ tr(v) ⊕ F_1^* ≅ tr(g) ⊕ (P_1 ⊕ Q_0)^*. The duals are finitely generated projective over R (Module.dual_projective, Module.dual_finite; (P ⊕ Q)^* = P^* ⊕ Q^* by Module.dualProdDualEquivDual); the contragredient S-structure (contragredient-dual) is a transport along the ring isomorphism σ and keeps both properties. The 'in particular' clause is proved simultaneously, with P = (Q_1 ⊕ P_0)^* and Q = (P_1 ⊕ Q_0)^*.

nodes.title: The Fitting ideal of the transpose
nodes.statement: (Dasgupta–Kakde Lemma 6.1.) Let R be a character group ring (more generally a commutative ring with a ring isomorphism σ : R^# → R) and M a quadratically presented R-module with square matrix (a_ij). The transpose M^tr attached to that presentation is quadratically presented over R^# with matrix (a_ji^#); this is the construction quadraticPresentation of PadicMeasuresIwasawaAlgebras:L6/presentation-transpose. The node asserts Fitt_{R^#}(M^tr) = Fitt_R(M)^#. The identity concerns the transpose of the stated quadratic presentation: adding a nonzero free relation summand makes the zeroth Fitting ideal of the transpose 0.
hypotheses: R is an arbitrary commutative ring; no noetherian or finiteness hypothesis is made beyond the stated ones.

Fitt_R(M) = Fitt^0_R(M) is the initial Fitting ideal of a finitely presented R-module M: the ideal generated by the n×n minors of the relation matrix of any finite presentation with n generators, independent of the presentation and compatible with base change. It is the finite-presentation Fitting-ideal carrier imported from the Tau Ceti roadmap StableReduction, Layer 1 (accepted RS-16).
For a ∈ R and an ideal J of R, a^# = σ^{-1}(a) ∈ R^# and J^# = σ^{-1}(J), an ideal of R^#; for R = R_Ψ and σ = # this is the notation of PadicMeasuresIwasawaAlgebras:L6/sharp-involution.
proofSteps: presentation-transpose (quadraticPresentation, quadraticPresentation_rel) gives the square presentation of M^tr with matrix (σ^{-1}(a_ji)) = (a_ji^#).
fitting-quadratic and det((a_ji^#)) = det(a_ij)^# (Matrix.det_transpose, and RingHom.map_det for the ring isomorphism #) give Fitt_{R^#}(M^tr) = (det(a_ij))^# = Fitt_R(M)^#.
acceptance: M = R/(x): M^tr = R^#/(x^#) and Fitt = (x)^#.
M = 0 presented by (1): M^tr = 0, Fitt = R^#.
M = 0 presented by R² → R, (a, b) ↦ a, which is not a quadratic presentation: the transpose is R^# and its zeroth Fitting ideal is 0, whereas Fitt_R(0)^# = R^# (R ≠ 0).

nodes.title: Higher Fitting ideals and transposes: free presentations
nodes.statement: Let R be a commutative ring with a ring isomorphism σ : R^# → R, and let R^t →A R^{t+s} → M → 0 be exact, A = (a_ij) a (t + s)×t matrix (t relations, t + s generators). Then the zeroth Fitting ideal over R^# of the transpose M^tr attached to this presentation is Fitt^s_R(M)^#: Fitt^0_{R^#}(M^tr) = Fitt^s_R(M)^#. Both ideals are generated by the t×t minors of A, resp. of the relation matrix (a_ji^#) of M^tr. The identity concerns the transpose of this presentation.
hypotheses: R is an arbitrary commutative ring; no noetherian or finiteness hypothesis is made beyond the stated ones.

Fitt_R(M) = Fitt^0_R(M) is the initial Fitting ideal of a finitely presented R-module M: the ideal generated by the n×n minors of the relation matrix of any finite presentation with n generators, independent of the presentation and compatible with base change. It is the finite-presentation Fitting-ideal carrier imported from the Tau Ceti roadmap StableReduction, Layer 1 (accepted RS-16).

Fitt^i_R(M) for i ≥ 1 is the higher Fitting ideal of PadicMeasuresIwasawaAlgebras:L6/higher-fitting-ideal. For a ∈ R and an ideal J of R, a^# = σ^{-1}(a) ∈ R^# and J^# = σ^{-1}(J), an ideal of R^#; for R = R_Ψ and σ = # this is the notation of PadicMeasuresIwasawaAlgebras:L6/sharp-involution.
proofSteps: M^tr = coker((R^{t+s})^* → (R^t)^*) is generated by the classes of the dual basis of (R^t)^* (presentation-transpose, mk_surjective). For the map Matrix.toLin' A the dual map sends e_i^* to Σ_j a_ij e_j^* = Σ_j σ^{-1}(a_ij) • e_j^* in the R^#-structure (LinearMap.toMatrix_transpose), and by mk_eq_zero_iff these t + s elements generate the relations. So M^tr is finitely presented over R^# with t generators and the t×(t + s) relation matrix (a_ji^#).

Fitt^0 of M^tr is generated by the t×t minors of (a_ji^#); Fitt^s of M, presented with t + s generators, by the minors of size (t + s) − s = t of A (PadicMeasuresIwasawaAlgebras:L6/higher-fitting-independence). A t×t minor of (a_ji^#) is the image under # of the corresponding minor of A (Matrix.det_transpose, RingHom.map_det), so # carries one generating set onto the other.
acceptance: s = 0, t ≥ 1 recovers transpose-fitting.
t = 0: M = R^s is free, M^tr = 0 and Fitt^s(R^s) = R = Fitt^0(0).
t = s = 1, A = (a, b)ᵀ: M = R²/R·(a, b) has Fitt^1(M) = (a, b); M^tr = R^#/(a^#, b^#) and Fitt^0(M^tr) = (a^#, b^#).

nodes.title: Higher Fitting ideals and transposes with excess generators
nodes.statement: (Dasgupta–Kakde (171), proof of Lemma B.4.) Let R be a commutative ring with a ring isomorphism σ : R^# → R, and let P_1 →f P_0 → M → 0 be an exact sequence of R-modules with P_1 and P_0 finitely generated projective of constant ranks t and t + s (locally t relations and t + s generators). Then the zeroth Fitting ideal over R^# of the transpose M^tr attached to f is Fitt^s_R(M)^#: Fitt^0_{R^#}(M^tr) = Fitt^s_R(M)^#. The identity concerns the transpose of this presentation. In Dasgupta–Kakde the presentation is V^θ → B^θ → ∇ → 0 over Z[G], with B^θ free of rank t + s and V^θ projective of constant rank t.
hypotheses: R is an arbitrary commutative ring; no noetherian or finiteness hypothesis is made beyond the stated ones.

Fitt_R(M) = Fitt^0_R(M) is the initial Fitting ideal of a finitely presented R-module M: the ideal generated by the n×n minors of the relation matrix of any finite presentation with n generators, independent of the presentation and compatible with base change. It is the finite-presentation Fitting-ideal carrier imported from the Tau Ceti roadmap StableReduction, Layer 1 (accepted RS-16).

Fitt^i_R(M) for i ≥ 1 is the higher Fitting ideal of PadicMeasuresIwasawaAlgebras:L6/higher-fitting-ideal. For a ∈ R and an ideal J of R, a^# = σ^{-1}(a) ∈ R^# and J^# = σ^{-1}(J), an ideal of R^#; for R = R_Ψ and σ = # this is the notation of PadicMeasuresIwasawaAlgebras:L6/sharp-involution.

A finitely generated projective module has constant rank t when its localisation at every prime ideal is free of rank t (Module.rankAtStalk). No freeness is assumed: over Z[G] a projective module of constant rank need not be free, and Z[G] is not a finite product of local rings.

M and M^tr are finitely presented, being cokernels of maps between finitely generated projective modules: such a module is finitely presented (Module.finitePresentation_of_projective), its dual is again finitely generated projective (Module.dual_finite, Module.dual_projective), and the quotient of a finitely presented module by a finitely generated submodule is finitely presented (Module.finitePresentation_of_surjective); the R^#-structure of M^tr is a transport along the ring isomorphism σ.
proofSteps: Two ideals of R^# are equal when they are equal after localising at every maximal ideal 𝔫 of R^# (Ideal.eq_of_localization_maximal). Put 𝔪 = σ(𝔫), a maximal ideal of R (Ideal.map_isMaximal_of_equiv); σ maps the complement of 𝔫 onto the complement of 𝔪 and so induces a ring isomorphism σ_𝔫 : (R^#)_𝔫 ≅ R_𝔪 compatible with σ (IsLocalization.ringEquivOfRingEquiv). Fitting ideals commute with base change (PadicMeasuresIwasawaAlgebras:L6/higher-fitting-base-change for Fitt^s, the imported carrier for Fitt^0), so Fitt^s_R(M)·R_𝔪 = Fitt^s_{R_𝔪}(M_𝔪) and Fitt^0_{R^#}(M^tr)·(R^#)_𝔫 = Fitt^0((M^tr)_𝔫).
The transpose commutes with base change (presentation-transpose, baseChangeEquiv), so (M^tr)_𝔫 is the transpose of f ⊗ R_𝔪 along (R^#)_𝔫 ≅ R_𝔪.

Over the local ring R_𝔪 the modules P_1 ⊗ R_𝔪 and P_0 ⊗ R_𝔪 are free (Module.Flat.of_projective, Module.free_of_flat_of_isLocalRing) of ranks t and t + s (Module.rankAtStalk; the localisation of P_i at 𝔪 is P_i ⊗ R_𝔪 by LocalizedModule.equivTensorProduct), so they have bases indexed by Fin t and Fin (t + s) (Module.finBasisOfFinrankEq). Choosing bases is an isomorphism of presentations, which does not change the transpose (presentation-transpose, equivOfIso), and the free case (PadicMeasuresIwasawaAlgebras:L6/transpose-higher-fitting-free) gives the equality at 𝔫.
acceptance: P_1 = R^t and P_0 = R^{t+s}: the statement is transpose-higher-fitting-free; with s = 0 and t ≥ 1 it is transpose-fitting.
t = 0: P_1 = 0, M ≅ P_0 is projective of constant rank s, M^tr = 0 and Fitt^s(M) = R = Fitt^0(0).

A presentation that is not free: R = R^# a Dedekind domain (σ the identity), I a nonzero ideal that is not principal, f the inclusion I ⊆ R (t = 1, s = 0). Then M = R/I, M^tr = I^{-1}/R, and both Fitting ideals are I.

Every term is free of rank 1, but the images in M_0 are p^mZ_p, a strictly decreasing chain: p^m is not in p^(m+1)Z_p since cancellation would make p a unit. The paper already records compactness of these unit modules in §9, printed p.163. Class-field-theory identifications remain separate inputs; the proposition’s conclusion is not refuted.

sourceIssues.locator: Remark 3.6, first sentence, published printed p.119 / PDF20; arXiv v2 p.14.
sourceIssues.printed: The remark claims completeness for each of the two topologies.
sourceIssues.correction: Retain norm completeness of the Banach dual. Do not claim completeness of the entire continuous dual for pointwise convergence; compact integral or bounded subsets require their own hypotheses and completeness statements.
sourceIssues.reason: Take B=c₀(ℕ,ℚ_p). Extend the algebraic functional e_n↦p^(−n) from the finite-support span to an algebraic linear functional ℓ on B using a vector-space basis. It is discontinuous because ‖e_n‖=1 while |ℓ(e_n)|=p^n. For each finite subset F of B, a finite set J of coordinates is injective on span(F): coordinate kernels separate points, and a descending chain of subspaces of that finite-dimensional space stabilizes. Extend ℓ|span(F) through the injection into ℚ_p^J to a linear functional on ℚ_p^J. Composing with coordinate projection yields a continuous functional ℓ_F on B agreeing with ℓ on F. Ordered by inclusion of F, these ℓ_F are eventually equal to ℓ at every fixed vector. Hence the net is Cauchy for pointwise convergence, but any weak limit would equal the discontinuous ℓ and could not belong to B*. This concerns completeness for nets, not a claim that every pointwise Cauchy sequence fails. The campaign already rejects unrestricted weak completeness.

sourceIssues.printed: The remark asserts that for any Dirichlet character η of conductor prime to p and exponents k ≡ ℓ modulo p^(m−1)(p−1), the values (1 − η(p)p^(k−1))L(η, 1−k) and (1 − η(p)p^(ℓ−1))L(η, 1−ℓ) are congruent modulo p^m, and applies this to the Riemann zeta function as the Kummer congruences.
sourceIssues.correction: Applying a congruence of test functions modulo p^m requires an integral bounded measure. For the trivial character the zeta object is a pseudomeasure; first clear its denominator with a smoothing factor, or state and prove the valid branch restrictions for an unsmoothed Kummer congruence.
sourceIssues.reason: Take p=3, m=1, η trivial, k=2 and ℓ=4. The exponents are congruent modulo p−1. Yet (1−3)ζ(−1)=1/6 and (1−27)ζ(−3)=−13/60, whose difference is 23/60 and has 3-adic valuation −1, not at least 1. Thus the blanket congruence, explicitly applied to the Riemann zeta function in the next sentence, is false. Clearing by [2]−[1] multiplies these two values by 2²−1 and 2⁴−1; the difference becomes 15/4, of valuation 1, as expected from the integral smoothed measure. No counterexample to the interpolation theorems or correctly qualified Kummer congruences is claimed. Arithmetic repairs belong to DirichletPadicLFunctions; this finding records the shared source distinction between bounded measures and pseudomeasures.
